title: The Computer
tagline: From counting beads to thinking machines in 5,000 years
intro: Look around you. There is probably a computer within arm's reach right now: in a phone, a laptop, a car key, a fridge or a game controller. But the word 'computer' once meant a person, usually with a pencil, doing sums all day long. How did we get from fingers and pebbles to machines that do billions of calculations every second? In these 20 parts you will slide beads on an abacus, crank the brass gears of Pascal and Babbage, read Ada Lovelace's daring notes, and follow Alan Turing into an imaginary machine that changed mathematics. You will sneak into wartime codebreaking huts, stand beside room-sized ENIAC, and watch the tiny transistor shrink computers onto chips smaller than a fingernail. Then come personal computers, phones, giant supercomputers and artificial intelligence, along with the problems they bring. Finally, we peek into the future. Ready? Let's boot up.

outline.title: Fingers, Pebbles and Beads
covers: Counting on fingers and tally marks; the Ishango bone from Central Africa (about 20,000 years old) as a POSSIBLE early tally stick, with its meaning still debated
Mesopotamian number writing on clay and the Babylonian base-60 system (why we still have 60 minutes and 360 degrees)
Counting boards and the abacus: the Greek Salamis tablet, the Roman hand abacus, the Chinese suanpan and the Japanese soroban; the word 'calculate' comes from Latin calculus, a small pebble
The Inca quipu: knotted strings used to record numbers in the Andes

The Antikythera mechanism: found in a Greek shipwreck in 1901, a geared device from roughly the 2nd or 1st century BCE that modelled the movements of the Sun, Moon and probably planets, and predicted eclipses
The idea of a 'tool that helps the mind', and that early tools stored numbers but the human still did the thinking
keyFacts: The Antikythera mechanism was recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in 1900–1901; X-ray CT scans in 2005 revealed thousands of tiny inscription characters and at least 30 surviving bronze gears
Nobody knows exactly where or when the abacus was invented; counting boards were used in Mesopotamia, Greece and Rome, and the bead suanpan was common in China by about the 1300s–1400s
Skilled abacus users can still add and subtract very quickly; the abacus remained in everyday use in shops in parts of Asia into the late 20th century
Babylonian scribes used a base-60 number system about 4,000 years ago
outline.hook: End with the question: what if the gears of a machine, not the fingers of a person, could do the adding?

outline.title: Gears That Do Sums
covers: John Napier's logarithms (1614) and 'Napier's bones' (1617) for multiplication
The slide rule, invented by William Oughtred in the 1620s and used by engineers until the 1970s
Wilhelm Schickard's 'calculating clock' (1623), described in letters to Johannes Kepler; the original was lost and later reconstructed from his sketches
Blaise Pascal's Pascaline (1642), built as a teenager to help his tax-collector father; the carry mechanism
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's stepped reckoner (designed from the 1670s) that could multiply, and his published work on binary arithmetic (1703)
Thomas de Colmar's arithmometer (patented 1820), the first calculator made and sold in large numbers
keyFacts: Pascal was about 19 when he began work on his calculator in 1642; about 20 Pascalines were made and around 9 survive
Leibniz published his paper explaining binary (base-2) arithmetic in 1703 and noticed patterns similar to the hexagrams of the Chinese I Ching
The arithmometer was produced commercially from about 1851 and several thousand were sold over the following decades
outline.hook: End by noting that machines could now add, but huge books of number tables were still made by hand, by people called computers.

outline.title: When Computers Were People
covers: 'Computer' was a job title: people who calculated tables for navigation, astronomy, banking and engineering
Predicting the return of Halley's Comet (1758–59): Alexis Clairaut, Jérôme Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute dividing up months of calculation
Gaspard de Prony's table-making project in revolutionary France (1790s), which split work like a factory into planners and many simple calculators
Britain's Nautical Almanac and how errors in printed tables could put sailors' lives at risk
The Jacquard loom (about 1804): punched cards that controlled woven patterns, building on earlier ideas by Basile Bouchon (1725) and Jean-Baptiste Falcon
The Harvard Observatory 'computers' of the 1880s onward, such as Williamina Fleming and Annie Jump Cannon, who classified stars
keyFacts: Clairaut's team predicted Halley's Comet would pass closest to the Sun in mid-April 1759; it did so in mid-March, within about a month of the forecast
A famous portrait of Joseph-Marie Jacquard was woven in silk on a Jacquard loom using about 24,000 punched cards; Charles Babbage owned a copy
Annie Jump Cannon classified hundreds of thousands of stars and helped create the star classification system still used today (O, B, A, F, G, K, M)
outline.hook: End with a young Englishman checking a book of tables, finding mistake after mistake, and wishing the calculations could be 'executed by steam'.

outline.title: Babbage's Engines
covers: Charles Babbage, mathematician and inventor, and the famous (reported) 1821 wish that tables could be calculated by steam
The Difference Engine (proposed 1822): the method of finite differences explained simply, so a machine only needs to add
Engineer Joseph Clement, government funding of about £17,000, and why work stopped in 1833 (a dispute and rising costs), leaving a demonstration piece
The Analytical Engine (designed from 1834): the 'mill' (like a processor) and the 'store' (like memory), punched cards borrowed from Jacquard, and the ability to make decisions based on results
Why it was never built in his lifetime; his son Henry Babbage later assembled part of the mill
The Science Museum in London building Difference Engine No. 2 from Babbage's drawings (completed 1991, printer added 2000), proving the design works
keyFacts: Difference Engine No. 2, finished in 1991 for the 200th anniversary of Babbage's birth, has about 8,000 parts, weighs about 5 tonnes and is about 3.4 metres long
Babbage designed Difference Engine No. 2 between 1847 and 1849
The Analytical Engine's store was planned to hold 1,000 numbers of 40 decimal digits each
outline.hook: End with Babbage meeting a brilliant young woman who understood his engine better than almost anyone: Ada Lovelace.

outline.title: Ada Lovelace and the Poetry of Numbers
covers: Ada Byron (later Countess of Lovelace), born 1815, daughter of the poet Lord Byron and mathematician Annabella Milbanke; her tutors including Mary Somerville and Augustus De Morgan
Meeting Babbage in 1833 at one of his parties and seeing the Difference Engine demonstration piece
Luigi Menabrea's 1842 French article on the Analytical Engine and Ada's 1843 English translation with her own Notes A to G, about three times longer than the article
Note G: a step-by-step method (an algorithm) for the engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers
Her big idea: the engine could work on any symbols, not just numbers, perhaps even music; and her caution that the engine cannot 'originate anything'
Fair credit: she is often called the first computer programmer; historians debate how much was hers and how much Babbage's, but the vision in the Notes is widely credited to her
Her death in 1852 at age 36, and her legacy: the Ada programming language (1980) and Ada Lovelace Day
keyFacts: Ada Lovelace was born on 10 December 1815 and died on 27 November 1852
Her translation with Notes was published in 1843 and signed only with her initials, A.A.L.
Babbage had sketched some programs for the engine before 1843, which is part of why historians debate the 'first programmer' title
outline.hook: End by saying that after Babbage died in 1871 his engines were mostly forgotten, but punched cards were about to return in a big way.

outline.title: Punched Cards, Logic and Brass Brains
covers: George Boole's algebra of logic (1847, 1854): TRUE and FALSE treated like numbers, which later became the basis of computer circuits
Herman Hollerith's electric tabulating machine for the 1890 US Census: holes in cards completed electric circuits and moved counting dials
Hollerith's Tabulating Machine Company (1896), which merged into a firm renamed IBM in 1924
Analog computers: Lord Kelvin's tide-predicting machine (1870s) and Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer at MIT (1931); the difference between analog (smooth quantities) and digital (counted steps)
Leonardo Torres Quevedo of Spain: his chess-endgame automaton (1912) and 1914 writings on automatic calculating machines
Offices filling with punched-card machines for payrolls, insurance and railways
keyFacts: The 1880 US Census took about 8 years to process by hand; with Hollerith's machines the first population count for 1890 was announced within a few months
Boole published 'The Laws of Thought' in 1854
Bush's differential analyzer weighed many tonnes and solved equations using rotating shafts, gears and wheel-and-disc integrators
outline.hook: End with a 23-year-old Cambridge mathematician asking a puzzling question: what exactly can be computed at all?

outline.title: Turing's Imaginary Machine
covers: David Hilbert's challenge, the 'decision problem' (Entscheidungsproblem): is there a mechanical method to decide any maths statement?
Alan Turing's 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers': an imaginary machine with an endless tape, a read/write head and a table of rules
The universal Turing machine: one machine that can imitate any other if given its rules as data, the seed of the idea of software
Some problems can never be solved by any computer (explain the halting problem simply)
Alonzo Church reached the same answer by a different route in 1936; Turing went to Princeton to study with him
Claude Shannon's 1937 master's thesis showing Boolean logic could be built from electrical switches and relays
keyFacts: Alan Turing was born on 23 June 1912 in London
Turing's paper was submitted in 1936 and published in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (1936–37)
Shannon's thesis, 'A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits', was written at MIT in 1937 and published in 1938
outline.hook: End by noting that while Turing imagined machines on paper, engineers in several countries were already building real ones, from relays and glowing tubes.

outline.title: Clicking Relays and Glowing Tubes
covers: Konrad Zuse in Berlin: the mechanical Z1 (1938) built in his parents' living room, and the Z3 (1941), a working programmable, binary, relay-based computer; the Z3 was destroyed in a 1943 air raid and later rebuilt
George Stibitz at Bell Labs: the 'Model K' relay adder (1937) built at his kitchen table, and the 1940 remote demonstration over telephone lines
John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry at Iowa State: the Atanasoff–Berry Computer (designed 1937–1942), electronic but not programmable
Howard Aiken's Harvard Mark I (built with IBM, working 1944), a huge electromechanical calculator controlled by punched paper tape
How relays (electromagnetic switches) and vacuum tubes (glass valves with no moving parts) work as on/off switches, and why tubes are much faster
Fair credit: there is no single 'first computer'; each machine was first in a different way
keyFacts: The Z3 used about 2,600 relays and was completed in May 1941
The Atanasoff–Berry Computer used about 300 vacuum tubes and stored numbers on rotating drums of capacitors
The Harvard Mark I was about 15 metres (51 feet) long and weighed about 4–5 tonnes
outline.hook: End with a war spreading across the world, and secret messages that only machines might be fast enough to crack.

outline.title: Codebreakers at War
covers: The German Enigma machine: rotors, plugboard and why its settings changed every day
The Polish Cipher Bureau: Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski first broke Enigma in 1932–33 and built the 'bomba' (1938); in July 1939 they shared their work with Britain and France
Bletchley Park in England: Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman designed the British Bombe (first working 1940), built by Harold 'Doc' Keen's team at the British Tabulating Machine Company
The harder Lorenz cipher ('Tunny'): Bill Tutte worked out its structure without ever seeing the machine; Max Newman's section

Tommy Flowers, a Post Office engineer, built Colossus, an electronic machine with about 1,600 (Mark 1) and 2,400 (Mark 2) vacuum tubes, working by early 1944 and the Mark 2 in time for D-Day, June 1944
The thousands of people, about three-quarters of them women (including Wrens of the Women's Royal Naval Service), who operated the machines; secrecy kept their work hidden until the 1970s
Colossus was programmable by switches and plugs but was a special-purpose codebreaking machine, not a general computer; a working rebuild was completed in 2007
keyFacts: About 10,000 people worked at Bletchley Park and its outstations by 1945
Ten Colossus machines were working by the end of the war in Europe; most were dismantled afterwards
Around 200 British Bombes were built during the war
outline.hook: End by crossing the Atlantic, where a giant American machine was being built to calculate artillery tables, and would become famous.

outline.title: ENIAC, the Giant Brain
covers: John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert at the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School, funded by the US Army to compute artillery firing tables
ENIAC's size and power: 17,468 vacuum tubes, about 27 tonnes, filling a large room, about 5,000 additions per second
Its public unveiling in February 1946 and newspaper headlines calling it a 'giant brain'
Programming by hand: plugging cables and setting switches, which could take days
The six original programmers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings (Jean Bartik), Betty Snyder (Holberton), Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas and Ruth Lichterman, and how they were overlooked for decades
Keeping tubes alive: failures, and running tubes at low power to make them last
The 1973 court case (Honeywell v. Sperry Rand) that ruled the ENIAC patent invalid, partly because of Atanasoff's earlier work
keyFacts: ENIAC used about 150 kilowatts of electricity and occupied about 167 square metres (1,800 square feet)
ENIAC was announced to the public on 14 February 1946 and was switched off for the last time in October 1955
One of ENIAC's first big jobs, in late 1945, was a calculation for nuclear weapons research at Los Alamos
outline.hook: End with a problem: to change ENIAC's program you had to rewire it. What if the program could be stored inside the memory, like the numbers?

outline.title: Machines That Remember Their Programs
covers: The stored-program idea: instructions kept in memory just like data, so a computer can switch jobs in seconds
John von Neumann's 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC' (1945), the 'von Neumann architecture', and the controversy because only his name appeared though Eckert and Mauchly shared the ideas

The Manchester 'Baby' (Small-Scale Experimental Machine) by Freddie Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill, which ran the first stored program on 21 June 1948, using a Williams tube (a TV-like screen) as memory
EDSAC at Cambridge (Maurice Wilkes, first ran 6 May 1949), the first stored-program computer in regular use for scientists; David Wheeler's subroutines
The first computers for sale: Ferranti Mark 1 (1951) and UNIVAC I (first delivered 1951), and UNIVAC predicting the 1952 US presidential election on TV
LEO I, built by the British tea-shop company J. Lyons, the first computer to run regular business jobs (1951)
keyFacts: The Manchester Baby had a memory of just 32 words; its first program ran for 52 minutes to find the highest factor of 2 to the power 18 (262,144)
UNIVAC predicted Eisenhower's landslide win in 1952 from early returns; the TV network at first doubted the prediction
Only about 46 UNIVAC I machines were built
outline.hook: End with the weak point of all these machines: hot, fragile vacuum tubes. In a New Jersey lab, three scientists were about to replace them.

outline.title: The Tiny Transistor
covers: Bell Labs: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain's point-contact transistor (December 1947) and William Shockley's junction transistor design (1948)
Semiconductors explained simply: materials like germanium and silicon whose ability to carry current can be controlled; a transistor as a switch with no moving parts
The 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for all three; Bardeen later won a second physics Nobel (1972)
Transistor radios (Regency TR-1, 1954) and the first transistor computers (Manchester 1953, Bell Labs' TRADIC 1954)
Magnetic-core memory (Jay Forrester and the Whirlwind computer at MIT): tiny rings of magnetic material storing 1s and 0s
Shockley's lab in California, the 'traitorous eight' who left in 1957 to start Fairchild Semiconductor, and the birth of what became Silicon Valley
keyFacts: The point-contact transistor was first shown to Bell Labs managers on 23 December 1947 and announced publicly on 30 June 1948
Gordon Teal at Texas Instruments made the first commercial silicon transistors in 1954
The 'traitorous eight' included Robert Noyce, Gordon Moore and Jean Hoerni
outline.hook: End with engineers drowning in wires: thousands of separate transistors had to be soldered together by hand. Could a whole circuit be made in one piece?

outline.title: Chips and the Computer on a Chip
covers: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrates the first integrated circuit on germanium (12 September 1958)
Robert Noyce at Fairchild designs a silicon integrated circuit (1959) using Jean Hoerni's planar process; both men are credited as co-inventors of the chip
The Apollo Guidance Computer (MIT Instrumentation Lab) as an early big user of chips
Gordon Moore's 1965 prediction ('Moore's law'): the number of components on a chip doubling regularly (every year, revised in 1975 to every two years)
Noyce and Moore found Intel in 1968

The Intel 4004 microprocessor (1971), designed for the Japanese Busicom calculator by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor and Masatoshi Shima; similar work at Texas Instruments and elsewhere around the same time; the Intel 8080 (1974)
keyFacts: The Intel 4004 had about 2,300 transistors and ran at about 740 kHz
Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000; Noyce had died in 1990, and Nobel Prizes are not given after death
The Apollo Guidance Computer used a few thousand identical simple chips, each containing logic gates
outline.hook: End by inviting the reader to shrink down and step inside one of these chips to see what really happens when a computer 'thinks'.

outline.title: Inside the Machine: Bits, Gates and the Clock
covers: Binary: why computers use only 0 and 1 (switches are reliable when they only have to be on or off); counting in binary; bits and bytes (8 bits)
Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) built from transistors, with everyday examples; how gates combine into an adder
The main parts: the CPU (control unit, arithmetic logic unit, registers), memory (RAM), storage, input and output; compare with Babbage's mill and store
The fetch–decode–execute cycle and the clock that ticks billions of times per second (gigahertz)
How chips are made: purified silicon, wafers, photolithography (printing patterns with light), clean rooms
Text, pictures and sound all turned into numbers (for example, letters as codes and images as grids of coloured pixels)
keyFacts: One byte (8 bits) can represent 256 different values (0 to 255)
A 3 GHz processor's clock ticks about 3 billion times per second
Modern laptop and phone chips contain tens of billions of transistors, and the largest AI chips more than 100 billion
outline.hook: End by pointing out that all this hardware does nothing on its own; it needs instructions written by people, called software.

outline.title: Teaching Machines to Understand Us: Software
covers: Machine code and assembly language, and why writing in raw numbers was slow and error-prone

Grace Hopper: the Harvard Mark II logbook moth (9 September 1947, 'first actual case of bug being found'), her A-0 compiler (1952) and FLOW-MATIC, which influenced COBOL (1959, designed by a committee)
FORTRAN (1957, John Backus's team at IBM) for scientists, LISP (1958, John McCarthy) and BASIC (1964, John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz at Dartmouth) for students
Mainframes and the IBM System/360 family (announced 1964); time-sharing letting many people use one computer through terminals

Space-age software: Dorothy Vaughan learning FORTRAN and teaching her team at NASA; Katherine Johnson checking the computer's orbit numbers for John Glenn's 1962 flight; Margaret Hamilton leading Apollo flight software, which handled the '1202' alarms during the Apollo 11 landing in 1969
Operating systems: UNIX (1969, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs) and the C language (about 1972)
keyFacts: Hopper's 1947 moth is kept at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History; engineers had already used the word 'bug' for faults since at least the 1870s
BASIC programs first ran at Dartmouth on 1 May 1964
Margaret Hamilton received the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016
outline.hook: End by noting that computers were still huge, expensive machines owned by governments, universities and big companies. Could one ever fit on a desk at home?

outline.title: A Computer on Every Desk
covers: Douglas Engelbart's 'Mother of All Demos' (9 December 1968): the mouse, windows, hypertext and video calls shown live
Xerox PARC's Alto (1973): a graphical interface with windows, icons and a mouse
The Altair 8800 kit (1975), the Homebrew Computer Club, and Bill Gates and Paul Allen founding Microsoft (1975) to make BASIC for the Altair
Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs founding Apple (1976); the Apple II, Commodore PET and Tandy TRS-80, the '1977 trinity'; VisiCalc (1979), the first spreadsheet program for personal computers
The IBM PC (1981) with Microsoft's MS-DOS, and the many 'IBM-compatible' clones
Home computers around the world: BBC Micro (1981), Sinclair ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64 (1982); kids learning to program at home
Time magazine's 'Machine of the Year' (the computer, for 1982) and the Apple Macintosh (1984) bringing a mouse-driven interface to the public
keyFacts: The Altair 8800 appeared on the cover of Popular Electronics magazine in January 1975 and was sold mainly as a kit
The IBM PC was launched on 12 August 1981
The Commodore 64 is often called the best-selling single computer model, with estimates of about 12 to 17 million sold
outline.hook: End by noting that once computers reached homes, they quickly spread into pockets, cars, toys and almost everything else.

outline.title: Computers Everywhere
covers: Games: Spacewar! (1962, MIT), Pong (1972, Atari) and home consoles; games pushing graphics hardware forward
Windows and point-and-click computing becoming normal (Windows 1.0 in 1985, Windows 95)
Portables and laptops: the Osborne 1 (1981) and later notebooks
Acorn's ARM chip (1985, designed by Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber), built to use very little power, now inside almost every smartphone
Smartphones: IBM Simon (1994), the iPhone (announced January 2007) and Android phones (2008); tablets
Hidden 'embedded' computers in cars, washing machines, medical devices and toys; the Raspberry Pi (2012) as a cheap computer for learning
How computers changed work (offices, design, factories, banking) and science; mention that the Internet and the Web have their own separate story
keyFacts: The first ARM chip ran correctly the first time it was switched on in April 1985
Tens of billions of ARM-based chips are shipped every few years; more than 250 billion had been made by the early 2020s
More than 60 million Raspberry Pi computers had been sold by 2024
outline.hook: End with a warning: anything this powerful and this everywhere also brings new problems.

outline.title: Bugs, Waste and Worries
covers: Famous software failures: the Ariane 5 rocket (1996) destroyed by a number too big for its variable; the Mars Climate Orbiter (1999) lost through a mix-up between metric and imperial units
The Y2K 'millennium bug': two-digit years, a huge worldwide repair effort, and why little went wrong on 1 January 2000
Computer viruses and malware, starting with early examples like Brain (1986); passwords, privacy and data being collected
Electronic waste and the mining of materials such as cobalt and tantalum, sometimes in harmful conditions; repair and recycling
Energy and water use of data centres and chip factories
Fairness: the digital divide; and how women, who did much early programming, became a smaller share of computer science students from the mid-1980s
Screen time and online safety, presented calmly and balanced
keyFacts: The world produced about 62 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2022, and only about 22% was documented as properly collected and recycled (Global E-waste Monitor 2024)
Data centres used about 1.5% of the world's electricity in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency
In the United States, women earned about 37% of computer science bachelor's degrees in the mid-1980s, falling to under 20% by the 2010s
outline.hook: End by turning to the most powerful computers of all: machines the size of a basketball court, and the new 'thinking' software they run.

outline.title: Supercomputers and Artificial Intelligence
covers: Seymour Cray: the CDC 6600 (1964) and the C-shaped Cray-1 (1976); FLOPS explained (calculations per second); the TOP500 list since 1993

Exascale: Frontier at Oak Ridge (2022) as the first machine officially to pass a quintillion calculations per second; El Capitan at Lawrence Livermore topping the list from November 2024; uses in weather, climate, medicine and physics
Turing's 1950 'imitation game' (Turing test) and the 1956 Dartmouth workshop where John McCarthy's group launched 'artificial intelligence' as a field; ups and downs called 'AI winters'
Milestones: IBM's Deep Blue beats chess champion Garry Kasparov (1997); AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go (2016)
Machine learning and neural networks explained simply: learning patterns from examples; GPUs from gaming powering the 2012 deep-learning breakthrough (AlexNet)
AlphaFold predicting protein shapes; chatbots built on large language models (ChatGPT, released November 2022); what AI can and cannot do, and why it can make confident mistakes
Nobel Prizes in 2024: Physics to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for neural network foundations; Chemistry partly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for AlphaFold (shared with David Baker)
keyFacts: The Cray-1 could perform about 160 million floating-point operations per second; Frontier passed 1 quintillion (a billion billion) per second
The first computer weather forecasts were run on ENIAC in 1950
Deep Blue won its 1997 rematch against Kasparov by 3.5 to 2.5; AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4 games to 1 in March 2016
outline.hook: End by asking what comes next when transistors are almost as small as atoms.

outline.title: The Next Computer, and the Long Road Here
covers: Moore's law slowing as features approach the size of a few atoms; new tricks such as 3D stacking and specialised chips

Quantum computers explained simply: qubits, Richard Feynman's 1981 idea, Peter Shor's 1994 algorithm, Google's 2019 'quantum supremacy' claim (disputed by IBM), and why they will help with some problems but not replace ordinary computers
Other experiments: brain-inspired (neuromorphic) chips, computing with light, and storing data in DNA
The big questions: energy use, fairness, jobs and keeping humans in charge of AI

Tying it together: the abacus stored numbers, Pascal's gears added, Jacquard's cards gave instructions, Babbage's mill and store became the CPU and memory, Lovelace saw symbols beyond numbers, Turing defined computing, and tubes, transistors and chips made it fast and small
A closing message: the computer was built by many people across many countries over thousands of years, and the reader could be one of the next
keyFacts: Shor's algorithm (1994) showed a large enough quantum computer could factor huge numbers quickly, which threatens some of today's encryption
Today's quantum computers have from dozens to around a thousand or so physical qubits, and errors are still a major challenge
ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes; a modern smartphone weighs about 200 grams and is millions of times faster
outline.hook: End the whole story with an invitation: the next part of the computer's story has not been written yet.

glossary: computer — today, a machine that follows a stored list of instructions to process information; before about 1950 it usually meant a person who did calculations
analog — working with smoothly changing quantities, like the angle of a gear or a voltage
digital — working with separate counted steps, usually the digits 0 and 1
binary — a number system using only two digits, 0 and 1
bit — one binary digit, a single 0 or 1; byte — a group of 8 bits
algorithm — a precise step-by-step method for solving a problem
program — a set of instructions telling a computer what to do; software is the general name for programs
relay — an electrically controlled switch with a moving metal contact
vacuum tube (valve) — a glass tube with no air inside that can switch or amplify electric current with no moving parts
transistor — a tiny switch or amplifier with no moving parts, made from a semiconductor (a material such as silicon whose ability to carry electricity can be precisely controlled)
integrated circuit (chip) — many transistors and connections made together on one small piece of silicon
microprocessor — a whole processor (CPU) on a single chip
CPU — the central processing unit, the part that carries out instructions; Babbage called it the 'mill'
memory (RAM) — fast working storage that holds programs and data while they are being used; Babbage called it the 'store'
logic gate — a tiny circuit that gives an output from inputs following a rule such as AND, OR or NOT
compiler — a program that translates code written in a human-friendly language into machine code
FLOPS — floating-point operations per second, a measure of how fast a computer does calculations with decimals
artificial intelligence (AI) — computer systems that perform tasks we usually think need human intelligence, such as recognising images or using language
machine learning — a way of making programs improve by finding patterns in lots of examples instead of following only hand-written rules
qubit — the basic unit of a quantum computer, which can be in a combination of 0 and 1 at the same time
doNotSay: Do not say any single machine was simply 'the first computer'; Z3, Atanasoff–Berry, Colossus, ENIAC and the Manchester Baby were each first in different ways
Do not say the abacus was definitely invented in China; its origins are uncertain and counting boards existed in Mesopotamia, Greece and Rome
Do not call the Antikythera mechanism a computer like ours or suggest it was alien or magical; it was a geared astronomical calculator
Do not say Pascal built the very first mechanical calculator; Schickard designed one earlier (1623)
Do not say Leibniz invented the idea of two-valued systems from nothing; he developed and published binary arithmetic
Do not say Jacquard invented punched control; Bouchon and Falcon used perforated paper and cards on looms earlier
Do not say Babbage built the Analytical Engine; it was never completed
Do not say Babbage's engines were impossible with Victorian technology; the 1991 Difference Engine No. 2 was built to tolerances achievable in his time
Do not say Ada Lovelace invented the computer, or state as undisputed fact that she wrote the very first program; say she is often called the first computer programmer and that historians debate it
Do not say Alan Turing alone broke Enigma or that he built Colossus; Polish codebreakers broke Enigma first and Tommy Flowers built Colossus
Do not repeat the myth that the Apple logo is a tribute to Alan Turing; its designer has said it is not
Do not claim certainty about how Turing died beyond what is recorded: the 1954 inquest ruled suicide and some people have questioned it; keep it brief and calm
Do not say Grace Hopper's moth was the origin of the word 'bug'; engineers used it for decades before 1947
Do not say Grace Hopper invented COBOL single-handedly; it was designed by a committee and drew heavily on her FLOW-MATIC
Do not repeat the legend that ENIAC dimmed the lights of Philadelphia when switched on as fact
Do not repeat unverified quotes as fact: Thomas Watson's 'world market for maybe five computers' and Bill Gates's '640K ought to be enough for anybody' have no reliable source
Do not say Apple or Microsoft invented the mouse or the graphical interface; Engelbart's team and Xerox PARC developed them first
Do not say Apple was built entirely in a garage; Wozniak has said the garage story is exaggerated
Do not say Moore's law is a law of physics; it is an observation and industry goal
Do not say chip names like '3 nm' mean transistors are 3 nanometres wide; they are marketing labels
Do not say computers or AI think, feel or understand exactly like human brains, or that AI is conscious
Do not say quantum computers will replace ordinary computers or are simply 'faster at everything'
Do not treat the Internet and World Wide Web as the same thing, and do not tell their history in detail; they have a separate story
Do not say Kilby or Noyce alone invented the chip; both are credited
